newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PM's calls won't bring big cut in Israeli rates.
newsitem.headline: PM's calls won't bring big cut in Israeli rates.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu made a political calculation in calling for interest rate cuts, but the central bank is unlikely to ease its monetary stance, analysts said on Tuesday.

"It indicates pressure and not a lot of clear-headed thinking," said Zvi Stepak, managing director of Meitav Securities. "He could have told (Bank of Israel Governor Jacob) Frenkel what he thought in private, but not in public. He's under a lot of pressure from industrialists on these issues."

At a meeting with business leaders and government officials on Monday, Netanyahu broke ranks with the central bank head whom he has publicly supported until now. "I am cutting the budget and I want you to reduce interest rates," he told Frenkel.

The prospects for a rate cut later this month strengthened with the release on Tuesday of a low September consumer price index of 0.4 percent, continuing a decelerating trend that began this summer. Housing prices, a key component of the CPI, fell 0.1 percent.

The Bank of Israel has been under immense pressure to reduce short-term rates, mainly because they have prevented the Israeli currency from depreciating in line with inflation. As a result, says David Levhari, professor of economics at the Hebrew University, the shekel is overvalued by six to seven percent.

This has made it difficult for Israeli exports to compete in world markets and has helped widen the country's current account deficit. But Frenkel has said he will maintain a tough monetary stance until inflation comes down and the government tightens fiscal policy.

The calls for rate cuts have taken on a new impetus with growing signs of a slowdown in the economy and a gradual fall in inflation, said Ptachia Bar Shavit, chief economist at Bank Hapoalim. He estimated consumer prices would rise 9.0 percent in 1997, versus 11.0-11.5 percent this year.

But analysts said Netanyahu's timing was a political calculation. At a marathon cabinet meeting that ran into early Monday morning, he convinced ministers to delay voting on a key clause in a capital-market reform package proposed by the Treasury that would have imposed taxes on short-term savings.
The decision was widely seen as a major defeat for Finance Minister Dan Meridor. Now, said Levhari, Netanyahu is seeking "a certain re-balance" by supporting a rate cut, which Meridor favors.
"I think this is less an economic matter than a psychological and political matter," he said.

In fact, the Bank of Israel has reduced the benchmark short-term rate from a peak of 17 percent in July to the current 15.5 percent. It will probably make further cuts because of falling inflationary expectations, said Bar Shavit.

However, the central bank is expected to keep to a target real interest rate of four to five percent, he said. The current nominal rate is at the top of the range, which leaves room for a reduction of up to one percentage point. But Bar Shavit doubted Frenkel would cut more because of Netanyahu's new stand.

"There is significant pressure on Frenkel, more than before," said Bar Shavit. "But this will not translate into a major reduction in interest rates. This month we'll probably see a cut of 0.5-0.7 percent."
The Bank of Israel will announce November rates at the end of October.
Frenkel would consider a deeper cut if the government reduces spending next year. "First and foremost, the government must cut the budget by five billion shekels," said Levhari.

The government plans to cut 4.9 billion shekels or 3.2 percent of next year's budget, although this still needs parliamentary approval. But Netanyahu has said further cuts may be needed in 1997 because of a short-fall in revenue.
